query: Review literature on grain-boundary thermal grooving in annealed metals (especially nickel) and its use for microstructure characterization: Mullins grooving theory and groove growth kinetics, groove dihedral-angle measurement of grain-boundary to surface energy ratios, thermal grooving as a way to reveal grain boundaries without metallographic preparation (etching/polishing), and the quality of EBSD/Kikuchi patterns obtainable from as-annealed (unprepared) surfaces. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

## 1. Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy

BibTex:

    author = "Bachmann, Björn-Ivo and Müller, Martin and Britz, Dominik and Durmaz, Ali Riza and Ackermann, Marc and Shchyglo, Oleg and Staudt, Thorsten and Mücklich, Frank",
    title = "Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy",
    year = "2022",
    journal = "Frontiers in Materials",
    volume = "9",
    month = "Oct",
    doi = "10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505",
    publisher = "Frontiers Media SA",
    issn = "2296-8016"
}


Abstract:
The high-temperature austenite phase is the initial state of practically all technologically relevant hot forming and heat treatment operations in steel processing. The phenomena occurring in austenite, such as recrystallization or grain growth, can have a decisive influence on the subsequent properties of the material. After the hot forming or heat treatment process, however, the austenite transforms into other microstructural constituents and information on the prior austenite morphology are no longer directly accessible. There are established methods available for reconstructing former austenite grain boundaries via metallographic etching or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) which both exhibit shortcomings. While etching is often difficult to reproduce and strongly depend on the investigated steel’s alloying concept, EBSD acquisition and reconstruction is rather time-consuming. But in fact, though, light optical micrographs of steels contrasted with conventional Nital etchant also contain information about the former austenite grains. However, relevant features are not directly apparent or accessible with conventional segmentation approaches. This work presents a deep learning (DL) segmentation of prior austenite grains (PAG) from Nital etched light optical micrographs. The basis for successful segmentation is a correlative characterization from EBSD, light and scanning electron microscopy to specify the ground truth required for supervised learning. The DL model shows good and robust segmentation results. While the intersection over union of 70% does not fully reflect the model performance due to the inherent uncertainty in PAG estimation, a mean error of 6.1% in mean grain size derived from the segmentation clearly shows the high quality of the result.

    title = "Investigation and Simulation of the Effects of nm-Scale γ′ Precipitates on the Recrystallization of Ni-based Superalloys",

    publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1073-5623"

Abstract:
Superalloys are critical materials for the hottest sections of stationary gas turbines and aircraft engines. Homogeneously fine-grained microstructures are essential to unlock their superior high-temperature strength but are challenging to achieve in γ ′-containing Ni-based superalloys. Such microstructures are achieved by recrystallization through hot working and grain boundary pinning via μ m-scale second phase particles. Discontinuous dynamic recrystallization is the predominant restoration mechanism, where grain growth is restricted by Zener pinning. Nanometer-scale γ ′ precipitates may exercise similar pinning during the nucleation stage and thus delay recrystallization. While the effects of coarse, μ m-scale, precipitates during recrystallization and grain growth are well-known, descriptions for fine coherent precipitates are currently lacking. To address this scarcity of knowledge, both γ ′-rich and -lean microstructures of the γ ′-containing Ni-base superalloy René 41 underwent identical uniaxial hot compression tests. Flow stress and microstructural analyses reveal the inhibition of recrystallization by nm-scale γ ′ precipitates during both nucleation and growth stages. This effect is successfully described using thermo-kinetic modeling through application of a driving-force based model. These unique insights provide a novel pathway to unlock homogeneously fine-grained microstructures in γ ′-containing Ni-based superalloys via advanced thermo-mechanical processing routes, required for applications in future generations of gas turbines and aircraft engines.

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000000

From text 'thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 11-13'.

Carl V. Thompson. Solid-state dewetting of thin films. Aug 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-matsci-070511-155048, doi:10.1146/annurev-matsci-070511-155048. This article has 1464 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses Mullins' theory of groove formation through curvature-driven surface self-diffusion at grain boundaries. According to this theory, groove depth scales with time as γ ∝(tDs)^(1/4), where Ds is surface self-diffusivity. Consequently, the time for hole formation (incubation time) scales as τn ∝ h^4/Ds, where h is film thickness. This kinetic process depends on both hole formation rate and hole growth rate. Regarding transport mechanisms, the excerpt clearly establishes that surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, though bulk self-diffusion and evaporation-condensation are theoretically possible. The flux of material due to curvature-driven surface self-diffusion is described mathematically, with material transported from high-curvature regions (grain boundaries) to lower-curvature areas, driven by differences in surface curvature.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses Mullins's pioneering theory of grain boundary (GB) grooving developed over fifty years ago for bulk bicrystals. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism for groove growth, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions. A key prediction of Mullins's theory is that GB grooves exhibit time-independent shape, meaning all linear dimensions of the groove grow with time according to the same power law. This theoretical framework has been widely used for determining surface diffusion coefficients from GB groove topography. The excerpt indicates that subsequent researchers have extended Mullins's model to binary alloys, considered grain boundaries as additional diffusion paths, and investigated anisotropy effects, but these developments generally maintained the original framework emphasizing capillary-driven surface diffusion as the dominant mass-transport mechanism.


---

## pqac-00000002

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a revised Mullins model for grain boundary grooving that incorporates both grain boundary (GB) and interface diffusion, departing from the original Mullins theory which assumed no diffusion flux at the GB root. The model governs the grooving process through a fourth-order partial differential equation: ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient, z is the surface profile, x is the spatial coordinate at the GB location, and t is annealing time. The solution exhibits self-similar kinetics with groove growth following z = m(Bt)^{1/4}F(u), indicating that groove dimensions scale as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width grow as t^{1/4}. The mechanism is surface diffusion, governed by the chemical potential gradient along the surface. The key modification from classical Mullins theory is replacing the zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant GB flux condition and zero curvature at the root, which ensures continuity of diffusion flux when GB and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion.


---

## pqac-00000003

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 4-6'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses grain boundary grooving mechanisms in thin films. Surface diffusion is identified as the dominant mass-transport mechanism for GB grooving. The authors rule out evaporation and evaporation-condensation mechanisms, noting that even with strong anisotropic behavior in surface energy and diffusivity, the theoretical timescales exceed the experimental annealing times. The kinetics are characterized through AFM measurements showing groove depth versus annealing time fitted by power law relationships. The excerpt also discusses how in strongly textured films, topography-changing surface diffusion may be inhibited due to low defect concentrations on singular (111) surfaces, necessitating consideration of alternative fast diffusion paths such as grain boundaries and interfaces. The study examines groove morphology in annealed Ni films, including the role of interface diffusion in the grooving process.


---

## pqac-00000004

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 6-7'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses classical Mullins theory of grain boundary (GB) grooving, which involves surface diffusion as the primary mechanism. In the Mullins model, material is extracted from the GB groove root and accumulated in two nearby ridges, conserving mass within the groove region. The classical Mullins groove exhibits a constant shape independent of absolute surface diffusivity values, with a width-to-depth ratio of approximately 30 for elemental metals like Ni. The excerpt contrasts this with observations in thin films where combined surface and GB diffusion, along with interface diffusion, produce grooves with positive mass imbalance and higher ridges than predicted by classical Mullins theory. However, the excerpt does not provide explicit kinetic equations for groove depth and width as functions of time, nor does it detail evaporation-condensation mechanisms. The text focuses on comparing classical Mullins behavior with observed deviations in thin film systems.


---

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000010

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This research demonstrates grain boundary (GB) grooving as a method to reveal grain boundaries in thin nickel films. The process occurs during thermal annealing at 700°C, where local film thickness decreases near grain boundaries due to energy minimization. The study shows that GB grooving is driven by the reduction of grain boundary area and concomitant decrease in total surface/interface energy. A key finding is that metal self-diffusion along the film-substrate interface contributes significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat grooves that deviate from classical theoretical predictions. The research indicates that GB grooving plays important roles in grain growth and thermal stability of thin films. However, the excerpt focuses on the mechanism and experimental observations rather than explicitly discussing advantages or disadvantages of this method compared to other grain boundary revelation techniques.


---

## pqac-00000011

From text 'bachmann2022efficientreconstructionof pages 2-3'.

Björn-Ivo Bachmann, Martin Müller, Dominik Britz, Ali Riza Durmaz, Marc Ackermann, Oleg Shchyglo, Thorsten Staudt, and Frank Mücklich. Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy. Frontiers in Materials, Oct 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505, doi:10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505. This article has 19 citations.

Thermal etching is a technique that can be used to delineate prior austenite grains (PAGs) in steel. However, it has notable drawbacks including the need for expensive equipment and the appearance of traces from old grooves created during the grain growth process. The excerpt indicates that while thermal etching is a viable method for revealing grain boundaries, these limitations have led to a preference for other approaches. Chemical etching techniques are generally preferred due to their simpler application without requiring special experimental devices, making thermal etching less commonly used despite its ability to reveal PAG boundaries.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Surface preparation significantly affects EBSD pattern quality and indexing confidence. The article emphasizes that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched specimens, as etching and surface roughness degrade diffraction patterns. High-quality EBSD patterns depend critically on removing lattice damage introduced during specimen preparation. Modern mechanical preparation methods can achieve excellent results without electrolytic or ion-beam polishing. The preparation quality can be verified using polarized light microscopy—if the polished surface produces high-quality polarized light images, it will yield EBSD patterns with high pattern quality indexes. Scratches and subsurface deformation must be completely removed, requiring careful sectioning, grinding, and polishing steps. Exceptional surface flatness is necessary due to the acute angle (70-74°) between specimen and electron beam. The article stresses that surface preparation damage directly influences indexing confidence.


---

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 3-5'.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt demonstrates that surface preparation significantly affects EBSD pattern quality and indexing capability. Proper mechanical polishing can produce damage-free surfaces yielding acceptable, indexable EBSD patterns. Surface relief caused by differential etching or inadequate polishing prevents EBSD pattern development from recessed phases. Vibratory polishing notably improves band contrast by an average of 11.1% and was essential for obtaining patterns from lead specimens. The comparison of Naval Brass samples shows that unetched, properly re-polished specimens produced excellent results for both phases, whereas etched specimens failed to generate patterns from the recessed beta phase. The preparation methodology is critical—proper execution enables reliable EBSD analysis across diverse metals and alloys ranging from magnesium to bismuth.

Mechanical preparation using proper multi-step polishing methods produces high-quality EBSD patterns. Vibratory polishing after standard preparation improves band contrast by at least 10%, with longer polishing times yielding further improvements. For copper alloys, etching followed by repeating the final polishing step reduces damage and produces better EBSD patterns. The study shows that damage from scratches and improper preparation degrades pattern quality. The excerpt indicates that high-purity metals and alloys are more difficult to prepare damage-free than commercial-purity metals, requiring careful attention to surface preparation. Overall, the work demonstrates that proper polishing and etching procedures are essential for obtaining quality EBSD patterns and successful indexing.

For example, pure lead yielded no EBSD pattern with standard methods but produced a pattern after one hour of vibratory polishing. Zirconium showed no pattern after chemical polishing alone. Table 4 demonstrates quantitative improvements in band contrast (a measure of EBSD pattern quality) from adding vibratory polishing: band contrast improved 3.8-20.9% across different elements (Pb showed improvement from no pattern to 108.0 band contrast). The study tested eighteen high-purity metal specimens using multi-step preparation protocols typically involving grinding with SiC paper followed by polishing with diamond suspensions and colloidal silica, indicating that careful surface preparation is critical for successful EBSD analysis.

This study examines grain boundary (GB) grooving in annealed nickel thin films, revealing that surface diffusion is the dominant mass-transport mechanism for GB grooving. However, in strongly textured films with low surface defect concentrations, topography-changing surface diffusion is inhibited, increasing the importance of alternative fast diffusion paths like grain boundaries and interfaces. The research demonstrates that both coupled surface and GB diffusion contribute to groove formation, with the observed groove morphology resembling profiles obtained theoretically under in-plane tensile stress. This interphase boundary diffusion can be as fast as or faster than GB diffusion itself. The authors developed a model incorporating both surface diffusion and metal atom diffusion along the Ni-sapphire interface to explain observed groove shapes that deviated from classical predictions. The simultaneous film thickening observed indicates that atoms diffuse along the interface, creating the characteristic groove topology that reveals grain boundary locations. Abstract:
<jats:p>We report a scalable route to hybrid aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) based on Al6060 (as-fabricated condition) reinforced with 2 wt.% TiB2 and 1 wt.% microsilica, fabricated by ultrasonically assisted stir casting (UASC) followed by radial-shear rolling (RSR). Premixing and preheating of powders combined with acoustic cavitation/streaming during UASC ensured uniform, non-sedimentary particle dispersion and low-defect cast billets. X-ray diffraction of the as-cast composite shows fcc-Al with weak TiB2 reflections and no reaction products; microsilica remains amorphous. Electron microscopy and EBSD after RSR reveal full erasure of cast dendrites, fine equiaxed grains, weakened texture, and a high fraction of high-angle boundaries due to the concurrent action of particle-stimulated nucleation (micron-scale TiB2) and Zener pinning/Orowan strengthening (50–350 nm microsilica). Mechanical testing shows that, in the cast state—comparing cast monolithic Al6060 to the cast hybrid-reinforced composite—yield strength (YS) increases from 61.7 to 77.2 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from 103.4 to 130.7 MPa, without loss of ductility. After RSR to Ø16 mm (cumulated true strain ≈ 0.893), the hybrid attains YS 101.2 MPa, UTS 150.6 MPa, and elongation ≈ 22.0%, i.e., comparable strength to rolled Al6060 (UTS 145.1 MPa) while restoring/raising ductility by ~9.7 percentage points. Microhardness follows the same trend, increasing from 50.2 HV0.2 to 73.1 HV0.2 when comparing the base cast condition with the rolled hybrid. The route from UASC to RSR thus achieves a favorable mechanical strength–ductility balance using an economical, eco-friendly oxide/boride hybrid reinforcement, making it attractive for formable AMC bar and rod products.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000029

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

EBSD requires an as-polished, non-etched specimen surface with exceptional flatness due to the steep angle (70-74°) between the specimen and electron beam. Surface roughness from etching degrades the diffraction pattern quality. The quality of EBSD patterns depends critically on removal of lattice damage from specimen preparation. Scratches and subsurface deformation must be completely removed, as damage depth affects pattern quality. The specimen preparation method should produce surfaces free of harmful residual preparation damage. Modern mechanical preparation methods can yield excellent EBSD patterns without electrolytic or ion-beam polishing. Quality is verified using polarized light microscopy—if metals show high-quality polarized light images without preparation damage, high-quality EBSD patterns with good pattern quality indexes will be obtained.


---

## pqac-00000030

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 3-5'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses critical surface preparation requirements for EBSD. Surfaces must be kept flat on the plane-of-polish, as relief causing one phase to recess below the surface prevents EBSD pattern development. Scratches and surface damage significantly affect pattern quality, requiring damage-free surfaces for reliable pattern indexing. Etching can be problematic—in Naval Brass, etching that attacked the β phase prevented EBSD patterns from the recessed phase, while unetched re-polished specimens produced excellent results for both phases. The preparation method described in Table 2 uses multiple polishing steps (240-grit through 0.05-μm colloidal silica) followed by vibratory polishing for optimization. Vibratory polishing alone improved band contrast by an average of 11.1% across tested elements. The article demonstrates that properly executed mechanical preparation produces damage-free surfaces yielding acceptable EBSD patterns, suggesting as-annealed surfaces require proper preparation but can ultimately provide good results.

EBSD achieves spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 µm for grain and subgrain characterization using FEGSEM. Angular resolution for automated EBSD typically ranges between 0.5° and 1.5° misorientations, with the lower limit achievable only from high-quality patterns with well-calibrated systems. Compared to TEM, EBSD can analyze several thousand subgrains from a single map with resolutions of ~0.5° for low angle grain boundaries, whereas TEM can measure misorientations as small as 0.1° but can only characterize far fewer subgrains from a thin foil. The choice between techniques depends on sample nature, the importance of detecting boundaries smaller than ~0.5°, and the scale of grain/subgrain structure. EBSD offers advantages for rapid automated analysis of large sample areas, while TEM provides superior angular precision for smaller misorientations but with more limited sampling.

EBSD provides spatial resolutions ranging from 9-180 nm depending on the material and microscope type (field emission gun vs. W-filament SEM), with field emission guns offering superior resolution. Angular precision for absolute crystallite orientation is typically ∼2°, though this varies with sample alignment and operating conditions. The angular resolution is influenced by probe current, accelerating voltage, and pattern quality. For characterizing low-angle grain boundaries, the precision of relative orientation measurements between adjacent data points is critical. EBSD represents an automated alternative to standard metallographic methods (optical and scanning electron microscopy) for obtaining grain sizes and shapes. However, limitations exist including non-indexed data points in deformed regions and difficulties determining small misorientations due to orientation noise, which can be quantified through apparent misorientations between data points within the same grain.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Topic | Key Findings | Key Parameters/Values | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mullins grooving theory fundamentals | Thermal grooves form where a grain boundary meets a free surface because capillarity drives material away from the groove root to reduce total interfacial energy. In the classical Mullins treatment, surface diffusion is the dominant transport path for small grooves, groove shape is self-similar, and mass removed from the root builds adjacent ridges. For elemental metals such as Ni, the classical groove has a large width-to-depth ratio. | Governing evolution is fourth-order diffusion-controlled surface smoothing/grooving; classical self-similar groove dimensions scale together; width-to-depth ratio for classical Mullins grooves is reported as about 30 for elemental metals such as Ni. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000025) |
| Groove growth kinetics | Mullins-type groove growth is diffusion controlled, with all linear dimensions increasing with the same power law. For surface-diffusion-controlled grooving, depth and width scale as \((Bt)^{1/4}\), so groove size follows a \(t^{1/4}\) law. This scaling underlies extraction of surface diffusion information from groove topography; in thin films, added grain-boundary or interface diffusion can accelerate or distort classical kinetics. | Groove depth and width \(\propto (Bt)^{1/4}\); incubation time for hole formation in films \(\tau \propto h^4/D_s\); dominant mechanism in solid films is usually surface self-diffusion rather than evaporation-condensation; modified Ni thin-film models include fast GB/interface diffusion. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000025) |
| Dihedral angle and energy ratio measurement | The equilibrium groove-root angle provides a direct route to the grain-boundary/surface-energy ratio through force balance. In isotropic form, the standard relation is \(\sin(\phi)=\gamma_{gb}/(2\gamma_s)\). In anisotropic form, the equilibrium condition includes the surface-energy derivative with orientation. In annealed Ni thin films, groove-profile fitting gave reasonable energetic values consistent with measured slopes. | Isotropic relation: \(\sin(\phi)=\gamma_{gb}/(2\gamma_s)\); anisotropic relation: \(0.5\gamma_{GB}=\gamma\sin\theta_0+(d\gamma/d\theta)\cos\theta_0\); representative Ni values used in fitting: surface energy \(\gamma_s \approx 1.8\ \text{J m}^{-2}\), grain-boundary energy \(\gamma_{gb} \approx 0.7\ \text{J m}^{-2}\), measured groove slope \(\sim 0.14\). | (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| Thermal grooving for grain boundary revelation | Thermal grooving/thermal etching can reveal grain boundaries without chemical etchants by generating topographic grooves during annealing. In Ni films, grooves directly delineate the grain-boundary network and can be measured by AFM/SEM. Advantages include chemically clean boundary revelation and simultaneous access to boundary energetics/kinetics; disadvantages include need for controlled high-temperature equipment, possible old-groove traces or evolving topography, and in thin films the complication of dewetting or interface-diffusion effects. Chemical etching is often simpler and cheaper for routine metallography. | Ni thin-film example: annealing at about 700 °C revealed GB grooves; groove morphology in Ni/sapphire deviated from classical Mullins behavior because interface diffusion contributed strongly; thermal etching in steels is useful but can leave traces of older grooves and needs specialized equipment. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027) |
| EBSD pattern quality and surface preparation requirements | The literature strongly indicates that EBSD is best performed on flat, damage-free, as-polished, non-etched surfaces. Surface relief, roughness, preferential attack, and preparation damage degrade Kikuchi patterns and indexing, so thermally grooved or otherwise topographic surfaces are generally unfavorable for high-quality EBSD unless subsequently repolished. Vibratory polishing materially improves pattern quality. EBSD remains powerful for grain-boundary characterization when preparation is adequate. | Vibratory polishing improved band contrast by about 11.1% on average; FEGSEM EBSD spatial resolution is about 0.1–0.2 µm; automated EBSD angular resolution is about 0.5–1.5° for relative misorientation; flat specimens tilted about 70–74° are required; etched/recessed phases may fail to yield patterns. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038) |

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.

- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective

    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.

    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,

- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.

## 1. Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy

    author = "Bachmann, Björn-Ivo and Müller, Martin and Britz, Dominik and Durmaz, Ali Riza and Ackermann, Marc and Shchyglo, Oleg and Staudt, Thorsten and Mücklich, Frank",
    title = "Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy",
    year = "2022",
    journal = "Frontiers in Materials",
    volume = "9",
    month = "Oct",
    doi = "10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505",
    publisher = "Frontiers Media SA",
    issn = "2296-8016"
}


Abstract:
The high-temperature austenite phase is the initial state of practically all technologically relevant hot forming and heat treatment operations in steel processing. The phenomena occurring in austenite, such as recrystallization or grain growth, can have a decisive influence on the subsequent properties of the material. After the hot forming or heat treatment process, however, the austenite transforms into other microstructural constituents and information on the prior austenite morphology are no longer directly accessible. There are established methods available for reconstructing former austenite grain boundaries via metallographic etching or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) which both exhibit shortcomings. While etching is often difficult to reproduce and strongly depend on the investigated steel’s alloying concept, EBSD acquisition and reconstruction is rather time-consuming. But in fact, though, light optical micrographs of steels contrasted with conventional Nital etchant also contain information about the former austenite grains. However, relevant features are not directly apparent or accessible with conventional segmentation approaches. This work presents a deep learning (DL) segmentation of prior austenite grains (PAG) from Nital etched light optical micrographs. The basis for successful segmentation is a correlative characterization from EBSD, light and scanning electron microscopy to specify the ground truth required for supervised learning. The DL model shows good and robust segmentation results. While the intersection over union of 70% does not fully reflect the model performance due to the inherent uncertainty in PAG estimation, a mean error of 6.1% in mean grain size derived from the segmentation clearly shows the high quality of the result.

    author = "Buerstmayr, R. and Theska, F. and Kozeschnik, E. and Webster, R. F. and Lison-Pick, M. and Street, S. and Primig, S.",
    title = "Investigation and Simulation of the Effects of nm-Scale γ′ Precipitates on the Recrystallization of Ni-based Superalloys",

    publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1073-5623"

Abstract:
Superalloys are critical materials for the hottest sections of stationary gas turbines and aircraft engines. Homogeneously fine-grained microstructures are essential to unlock their superior high-temperature strength but are challenging to achieve in γ ′-containing Ni-based superalloys. Such microstructures are achieved by recrystallization through hot working and grain boundary pinning via μ m-scale second phase particles. Discontinuous dynamic recrystallization is the predominant restoration mechanism, where grain growth is restricted by Zener pinning. Nanometer-scale γ ′ precipitates may exercise similar pinning during the nucleation stage and thus delay recrystallization. While the effects of coarse, μ m-scale, precipitates during recrystallization and grain growth are well-known, descriptions for fine coherent precipitates are currently lacking. To address this scarcity of knowledge, both γ ′-rich and -lean microstructures of the γ ′-containing Ni-base superalloy René 41 underwent identical uniaxial hot compression tests. Flow stress and microstructural analyses reveal the inhibition of recrystallization by nm-scale γ ′ precipitates during both nucleation and growth stages. This effect is successfully described using thermo-kinetic modeling through application of a driving-force based model. These unique insights provide a novel pathway to unlock homogeneously fine-grained microstructures in γ ′-containing Ni-based superalloys via advanced thermo-mechanical processing routes, required for applications in future generations of gas turbines and aircraft engines.

Carl V. Thompson. Solid-state dewetting of thin films. Aug 2012. URL: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-matsci-070511-155048, doi:10.1146/annurev-matsci-070511-155048. This article has 1464 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses Mullins' theory of groove formation through curvature-driven surface self-diffusion at grain boundaries. According to this theory, groove depth scales with time as γ ∝(tDs)^(1/4), where Ds is surface self-diffusivity. Consequently, the time for hole formation (incubation time) scales as τn ∝ h^4/Ds, where h is film thickness. This kinetic process depends on both hole formation rate and hole growth rate. Regarding transport mechanisms, the excerpt clearly establishes that surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, though bulk self-diffusion and evaporation-condensation are theoretically possible. The flux of material due to curvature-driven surface self-diffusion is described mathematically, with material transported from high-curvature regions (grain boundaries) to lower-curvature areas, driven by differences in surface curvature.

The excerpt discusses Mullins's pioneering theory of grain boundary (GB) grooving developed over fifty years ago for bulk bicrystals. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism for groove growth, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions. A key prediction of Mullins's theory is that GB grooves exhibit time-independent shape, meaning all linear dimensions of the groove grow with time according to the same power law. This theoretical framework has been widely used for determining surface diffusion coefficients from GB groove topography. The excerpt indicates that subsequent researchers have extended Mullins's model to binary alloys, considered grain boundaries as additional diffusion paths, and investigated anisotropy effects, but these developments generally maintained the original framework emphasizing capillary-driven surface diffusion as the dominant mass-transport mechanism.

The excerpt describes a revised Mullins model for grain boundary grooving that incorporates both grain boundary (GB) and interface diffusion, departing from the original Mullins theory which assumed no diffusion flux at the GB root. The model governs the grooving process through a fourth-order partial differential equation: ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient, z is the surface profile, x is the spatial coordinate at the GB location, and t is annealing time. The solution exhibits self-similar kinetics with groove growth following z = m(Bt)^{1/4}F(u), indicating that groove dimensions scale as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width grow as t^{1/4}. The mechanism is surface diffusion, governed by the chemical potential gradient along the surface. The key modification from classical Mullins theory is replacing the zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant GB flux condition and zero curvature at the root, which ensures continuity of diffusion flux when GB and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion.

The excerpt discusses classical Mullins theory of grain boundary (GB) grooving, which involves surface diffusion as the primary mechanism. In the Mullins model, material is extracted from the GB groove root and accumulated in two nearby ridges, conserving mass within the groove region. The classical Mullins groove exhibits a constant shape independent of absolute surface diffusivity values, with a width-to-depth ratio of approximately 30 for elemental metals like Ni. The excerpt contrasts this with observations in thin films where combined surface and GB diffusion, along with interface diffusion, produce grooves with positive mass imbalance and higher ridges than predicted by classical Mullins theory. However, the excerpt does not provide explicit kinetic equations for groove depth and width as functions of time, nor does it detail evaporation-condensation mechanisms. The text focuses on comparing classical Mullins behavior with observed deviations in thin film systems.

This excerpt discusses modifications to the Mullins model of thermal grain boundary grooving. The original Mullins model focuses on groove growth by surface diffusion alone. The authors modified this model to account for fast grain boundary (GB) and interphase boundary diffusion. A key finding is that GB grooves growing by a combination of surface, GB, and interface diffusion mechanisms deepen faster than classical Mullins-type grooves that rely on surface diffusion alone. The paper establishes that among diffusion paths in crystalline solids, the hierarchy from slowest to fastest is: bulk diffusion, dislocation core diffusion, GB diffusion, and surface diffusion. Notably, the research demonstrates that metal self-diffusion along metal-ceramic interfaces can be faster than mass-transporting surface self-diffusion. The excerpt does not provide detailed kinetic equations for groove depth and width as functions of time, but emphasizes the importance of interface diffusion as an additional transport mechanism beyond the classical surface diffusion mechanism in the Mullins model.

The authors extend Mullins's isotropic model of GB grooving to account for both grain boundary and interface diffusion contributions to mass transport. The excerpt presents the equilibrium condition at the groove root that relates the grain boundary energy (cGB) to surface energy (c) through the surface slope angle (h0) at the groove root. Equation (25) shows that 0.5cGB = c sin h0 + (dc/dh) cos h0, which is the fundamental relation describing groove equilibrium. From this equilibrium condition, equation (26) derives the maximum surface slope: sin h0 = (0.5cGB - Dc)/(c0), where c0 is the surface energy at the singular surface and Dc represents the anisotropy. The dihedral angle at the groove root (related to h0) thus provides a way to measure the ratio of grain boundary energy to surface energy through these equilibrium relations. The text indicates these relations account for both isotropic surface energy and orientation-dependent anisotropy effects.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2'.

D. Amram, L. Klinger, Nimrod Gazit, H. Gluska, and E. Rabkin. Grain boundary grooving in thin films revisited: the role of interface diffusion. Acta Materialia, 69:386-396, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2014.02.008. This article has 127 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This research demonstrates grain boundary (GB) grooving as a method to reveal grain boundaries in thin nickel films. The process occurs during thermal annealing at 700°C, where local film thickness decreases near grain boundaries due to energy minimization. The study shows that GB grooving is driven by the reduction of grain boundary area and concomitant decrease in total surface/interface energy. A key finding is that metal self-diffusion along the film-substrate interface contributes significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat grooves that deviate from classical theoretical predictions. The research indicates that GB grooving plays important roles in grain growth and thermal stability of thin films. However, the excerpt focuses on the mechanism and experimental observations rather than explicitly discussing advantages or disadvantages of this method compared to other grain boundary revelation techniques.


---

## pqac-00000011

From text 'bachmann2022efficientreconstructionof pages 2-3'.

Björn-Ivo Bachmann, Martin Müller, Dominik Britz, Ali Riza Durmaz, Marc Ackermann, Oleg Shchyglo, Thorsten Staudt, and Frank Mücklich. Efficient reconstruction of prior austenite grains in steel from etched light optical micrographs using deep learning and annotations from correlative microscopy. Frontiers in Materials, Oct 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505, doi:10.3389/fmats.2022.1033505. This article has 19 citations.

Thermal etching is a technique that can be used to delineate prior austenite grains (PAGs) in steel. However, it has notable drawbacks including the need for expensive equipment and the appearance of traces from old grooves created during the grain growth process. The excerpt indicates that while thermal etching is a viable method for revealing grain boundaries, these limitations have led to a preference for other approaches. Chemical etching techniques are generally preferred due to their simpler application without requiring special experimental devices, making thermal etching less commonly used despite its ability to reveal PAG boundaries.
