## pqac-00000012

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Surface preparation significantly affects EBSD pattern quality and indexing confidence. The article emphasizes that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched specimens, as etching and surface roughness degrade diffraction patterns. High-quality EBSD patterns depend critically on removing lattice damage introduced during specimen preparation. Modern mechanical preparation methods can achieve excellent results without electrolytic or ion-beam polishing. The preparation quality can be verified using polarized light microscopy—if the polished surface produces high-quality polarized light images, it will yield EBSD patterns with high pattern quality indexes. Scratches and subsurface deformation must be completely removed, requiring careful sectioning, grinding, and polishing steps. Exceptional surface flatness is necessary due to the acute angle (70-74°) between specimen and electron beam. The article stresses that surface preparation damage directly influences indexing confidence.


---

## pqac-00000013

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 3-5'.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt demonstrates that surface preparation significantly affects EBSD pattern quality and indexing capability. Proper mechanical polishing can produce damage-free surfaces yielding acceptable, indexable EBSD patterns. Surface relief caused by differential etching or inadequate polishing prevents EBSD pattern development from recessed phases. Vibratory polishing notably improves band contrast by an average of 11.1% and was essential for obtaining patterns from lead specimens. The comparison of Naval Brass samples shows that unetched, properly re-polished specimens produced excellent results for both phases, whereas etched specimens failed to generate patterns from the recessed beta phase. The preparation methodology is critical—proper execution enables reliable EBSD analysis across diverse metals and alloys ranging from magnesium to bismuth.

Mechanical preparation using proper multi-step polishing methods produces high-quality EBSD patterns. Vibratory polishing after standard preparation improves band contrast by at least 10%, with longer polishing times yielding further improvements. For copper alloys, etching followed by repeating the final polishing step reduces damage and produces better EBSD patterns. The study shows that damage from scratches and improper preparation degrades pattern quality. The excerpt indicates that high-purity metals and alloys are more difficult to prepare damage-free than commercial-purity metals, requiring careful attention to surface preparation. Overall, the work demonstrates that proper polishing and etching procedures are essential for obtaining quality EBSD patterns and successful indexing.

This metallographic preparation study demonstrates that surface preparation significantly affects EBSD pattern quality. The excerpt does not directly address unprepared or as-annealed surfaces. However, it shows that specific polishing methods are essential for obtaining diffraction patterns. For example, pure lead yielded no EBSD pattern with standard methods but produced a pattern after one hour of vibratory polishing. Zirconium showed no pattern after chemical polishing alone. Table 4 demonstrates quantitative improvements in band contrast (a measure of EBSD pattern quality) from adding vibratory polishing: band contrast improved 3.8-20.9% across different elements (Pb showed improvement from no pattern to 108.0 band contrast). The study tested eighteen high-purity metal specimens using multi-step preparation protocols typically involving grinding with SiC paper followed by polishing with diamond suspensions and colloidal silica, indicating that careful surface preparation is critical for successful EBSD analysis.

The groove depth (δ) formed at grain boundaries depends on the grain radius (R) and the root angle (ϕ), which is determined by a force balance between the grain boundary energy (γgb) and film surface energy (γf). The groove profile shape is directly determined by the energies of surfaces meeting at the grain boundary and the grain boundary energy itself. Critically, hole formation and dewetting initiation occurs only when groove depth exceeds film thickness (δ > h). When δ is less than film thickness, grooves remain stable without initiating rupture. The critical grain radius for hole formation is given by a function of these geometric and energetic parameters.

Abstract:
<jats:p>We report a scalable route to hybrid aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) based on Al6060 (as-fabricated condition) reinforced with 2 wt.% TiB2 and 1 wt.% microsilica, fabricated by ultrasonically assisted stir casting (UASC) followed by radial-shear rolling (RSR). Premixing and preheating of powders combined with acoustic cavitation/streaming during UASC ensured uniform, non-sedimentary particle dispersion and low-defect cast billets. X-ray diffraction of the as-cast composite shows fcc-Al with weak TiB2 reflections and no reaction products; microsilica remains amorphous. Electron microscopy and EBSD after RSR reveal full erasure of cast dendrites, fine equiaxed grains, weakened texture, and a high fraction of high-angle boundaries due to the concurrent action of particle-stimulated nucleation (micron-scale TiB2) and Zener pinning/Orowan strengthening (50–350 nm microsilica). Mechanical testing shows that, in the cast state—comparing cast monolithic Al6060 to the cast hybrid-reinforced composite—yield strength (YS) increases from 61.7 to 77.2 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from 103.4 to 130.7 MPa, without loss of ductility. After RSR to Ø16 mm (cumulated true strain ≈ 0.893), the hybrid attains YS 101.2 MPa, UTS 150.6 MPa, and elongation ≈ 22.0%, i.e., comparable strength to rolled Al6060 (UTS 145.1 MPa) while restoring/raising ductility by ~9.7 percentage points. Microhardness follows the same trend, increasing from 50.2 HV0.2 to 73.1 HV0.2 when comparing the base cast condition with the rolled hybrid. The route from UASC to RSR thus achieves a favorable mechanical strength–ductility balance using an economical, eco-friendly oxide/boride hybrid reinforcement, making it attractive for formable AMC bar and rod products.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000029

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

EBSD requires an as-polished, non-etched specimen surface with exceptional flatness due to the steep angle (70-74°) between the specimen and electron beam. Surface roughness from etching degrades the diffraction pattern quality. The quality of EBSD patterns depends critically on removal of lattice damage from specimen preparation. Scratches and subsurface deformation must be completely removed, as damage depth affects pattern quality. The specimen preparation method should produce surfaces free of harmful residual preparation damage. Modern mechanical preparation methods can yield excellent EBSD patterns without electrolytic or ion-beam polishing. Quality is verified using polarized light microscopy—if metals show high-quality polarized light images without preparation damage, high-quality EBSD patterns with good pattern quality indexes will be obtained.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 3-5'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses critical surface preparation requirements for EBSD. Surfaces must be kept flat on the plane-of-polish, as relief causing one phase to recess below the surface prevents EBSD pattern development. Scratches and surface damage significantly affect pattern quality, requiring damage-free surfaces for reliable pattern indexing. Etching can be problematic—in Naval Brass, etching that attacked the β phase prevented EBSD patterns from the recessed phase, while unetched re-polished specimens produced excellent results for both phases. The preparation method described in Table 2 uses multiple polishing steps (240-grit through 0.05-μm colloidal silica) followed by vibratory polishing for optimization. Vibratory polishing alone improved band contrast by an average of 11.1% across tested elements. The article demonstrates that properly executed mechanical preparation produces damage-free surfaces yielding acceptable EBSD patterns, suggesting as-annealed surfaces require proper preparation but can ultimately provide good results.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 2-3'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes surface preparation requirements for EBSD analysis. Proper mechanical preparation using multi-step methods (3-5 steps) is essential for producing high-quality EBSD patterns. Surface damage from grinding and sectioning significantly impacts pattern quality; scratch removal is particularly critical for ductile materials like pure copper and brass. Vibratory polishing with colloidal silica following standard preparation improves results by removing scratches and subsurface damage, increasing band contrast by at least 10%. The plane-of-polish orientation (70-74° from horizontal) is important for EBSD systems. The excerpt indicates that etching followed by repeat polishing reduces damage and improves EBSD patterns. High-purity metals are more difficult to prepare than commercial-purity metals. The text demonstrates successful EBSD pattern generation on cast and wrought aluminum samples, suggesting EBSD can be performed on various microstructural conditions when properly prepared.

From text 'voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 5-7'.

G Vander Voort, W Van Geertruyden, S Dillon, and E Manilova. Metallographic preparation for electron backscattered diffraction. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 12:1610-1611, Jul 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927606069327, doi:10.1017/s1431927606069327. This article has 39 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes detailed metallographic preparation methods for EBSD analysis of high-purity metals. Surface preparation involves multi-step grinding and polishing procedures, typically five steps (four for Ti). For certain elements susceptible to SiC embedment (Sb, V, Zr), grinding paper was coated with paraffin wax. Attack polishing with 30% H2O2 was used as a final step for Cr, Nb, Ti, W, and Zr. Final polishing employed MasterMet® colloidal silica for most specimens. The excerpt demonstrates that surface condition significantly affects EBSD pattern quality. Chemical polishing of Zr improved polarized light response but introduced excessive relief/grain faceting, which prevented obtaining EBSD patterns on the chemically polished surface. The preparation method directly impacts band contrast and indexable pixel percentages—the improved method achieved 92.34 average band contrast with ~90% indexable pixels versus 77.3 with only ~20% indexable pixels using less effective methods. Vibratory polishing further improved band contrast across multiple high-purity elements.

The excerpt provides limited information on surface preparation for EBSD. It indicates that electropolished surfaces are often required, though good mechanical polish is sufficient for hard materials. The diffraction pattern originates from the surface layer. In multi-phase alloys, preferential polishing of one phase can cause shadowing effects due to the large tilt angle. The specimen region must have a single crystallographic orientation to obtain an analyzable pattern. Defects such as dislocations can cause pattern sharpness loss, but the pattern remains analyzable unless damage is severe. However, the excerpt does not specifically address the effects of surface roughness, oxidation, etching, or whether EBSD can be performed on as-annealed surfaces.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 12-13'.

F. J. Humphreys. Review grain and subgrain characterisation by electron backscatter diffraction. Journal of Materials Science, 36:3833-3854, Aug 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1017973432592, doi:10.1023/a:1017973432592. This article has 1472 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

EBSD achieves spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 µm for grain and subgrain characterization using FEGSEM. Angular resolution for automated EBSD typically ranges between 0.5° and 1.5° misorientations, with the lower limit achievable only from high-quality patterns with well-calibrated systems. Compared to TEM, EBSD can analyze several thousand subgrains from a single map with resolutions of ~0.5° for low angle grain boundaries, whereas TEM can measure misorientations as small as 0.1° but can only characterize far fewer subgrains from a thin foil. The choice between techniques depends on sample nature, the importance of detecting boundaries smaller than ~0.5°, and the scale of grain/subgrain structure. {"answer": "# Grain-Boundary Thermal Grooving in Annealed Metals: Theory, Energy Measurements, Microstructure Revelation, and EBSD Characterization

## 1. Mullins Grooving Theory and Groove Growth Kinetics

The classical theory of grain-boundary thermal grooving was developed by Mullins in 1957, providing the foundational framework for understanding how grooves form where grain boundaries intersect free surfaces during annealing. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism governing groove development, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions (pqac-00000001). The governing equation for the surface profile evolution is a fourth-order partial differential equation of the form ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient that incorporates surface diffusivity, surface energy, atomic volume, and temperature (pqac-00000002).

A central prediction of the Mullins theory is that the groove profile exhibits a self-similar shape: all linear dimensions of the groove (depth, width) grow according to the same power law, scaling as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width increase proportional to t^{1/4} (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000000). In the classical model, material is extracted from the groove root and deposited in two characteristic ridges flanking the groove, conserving mass within the groove region; for elemental metals such as nickel, the classical groove width-to-depth ratio is approximately 30 (pqac-00000004). The time for hole formation through grooving in thin films scales with the fourth power of film thickness: τ_n ∝ h⁴/D_s, where h is the film thickness and D_s is the surface self-diffusivity (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025).

While surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, Mullins also considered evaporation-condensation as an alternative transport mechanism (pqac-00000006). However, for most metallic systems, surface diffusion dominates. Mullins introduced a dimensionless parameter r to characterize the ratio of material removed by surface diffusion versus evaporation; when r > 10², surface diffusion is the controlling mechanism (pqac-00000006).

Important extensions to the classical theory have been developed. Amram et al. (2014) demonstrated that in thin nickel films on sapphire substrates annealed at 700°C, grain-boundary and metal-ceramic interface diffusion contribute significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat, ridge-less grooves that deviate from classical Mullins predictions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000027). Their modified model replaces the classical zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant grain-boundary flux condition and zero curvature at the root, reflecting the fact that grain-boundary and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000021). The hierarchy of diffusion paths in crystalline solids, from slowest to fastest, is: bulk diffusion, dislocation core diffusion, grain-boundary diffusion, and surface diffusion (pqac-00000005).

## 2. Groove Dihedral-Angle Measurement and Grain-Boundary to Surface Energy Ratios

The equilibrium geometry at the groove root provides a direct means of measuring the ratio of grain-boundary energy (γ_gb) to surface energy (γ_s). At the groove root, a force balance between the grain boundary and the two free surfaces establishes the dihedral angle φ. In the isotropic case, the equilibrium condition yields the classical relation:

sin(φ) = γ_gb / (2γ_s)

This relationship allows the grain-boundary to surface energy ratio to be extracted from measurements of the groove-root dihedral angle (pqac-00000008). The groove depth δ can then be related to the grain radius R and dihedral angle through geometric relationships (pqac-00000023).

When surface energy anisotropy is significant, as in strongly textured nickel films, the equilibrium condition at the groove root must be generalized to account for the orientation-dependence of surface energy. The anisotropic form is:

0.5γ_GB = γ sin(θ_0) + (dγ/dθ) cos(θ_0)

where θ_0 is the maximum surface slope at the groove root, γ is the orientation-dependent surface energy, and the derivative term captures the torque contribution from surface energy anisotropy (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). From this equilibrium expression, the maximum surface slope can be derived as sin(θ_0) = (0.5γ_GB − Δγ)/γ_0, where γ_0 is the surface energy at the singular surface orientation and Δγ represents the anisotropy (pqac-00000007).

For nickel specifically, Amram et al. (2014) fitted experimental groove profiles measured by atomic force microscopy (AFM) to their theoretical model, finding excellent agreement when using representative energy values of γ_0 ≈ 1.8 J m⁻², Δγ ≈ 0.1 J m⁻², and γ_GB ≈ 0.7 J m⁻², with observed groove slopes of approximately 0.14 (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000042). The method has been widely applied to measure relative grain-boundary energies in various polycrystalline materials.

## 3. Thermal Grooving as a Means to Reveal Grain Boundaries Without Metallographic Preparation

Thermal grooving (also termed thermal etching) provides a route to reveal grain boundaries without recourse to chemical etchants. During annealing, surface diffusion drives groove formation at grain-boundary/surface junctions, creating topographic features that delineate the grain-boundary network and are readily observable by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), optical microscopy, or AFM (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018).

In nickel thin films, annealing at approximately 700°C produces well-defined grooves that clearly reveal the grain structure, including the mazed bicrystal microstructure characteristic of strongly textured films (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000017). The technique simultaneously provides quantitative information about boundary energetics and diffusion kinetics that chemical etching cannot deliver. In polycrystalline thin films more generally, grain-boundary grooves form preferentially at high-energy boundaries and triple junctions, with groove depth varying with local grain-boundary energy (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028). The process is also observed in silver thin films, where thermal grooves at grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for dewetting (pqac-00000020).

Despite these advantages, thermal etching has notable practical drawbacks. Bachmann et al. (2022) noted that in steels, thermal etching requires expensive high-temperature equipment and produces traces of old grooves from grain growth during the heating process, complicating interpretation (pqac-00000011). Chemical etching is generally preferred for routine metallography because it is simpler, less costly, and does not require controlled high-temperature environments (pqac-00000011). Additionally, in thin-film systems, thermal grooving can be complicated by concurrent dewetting, interface diffusion effects, and oxide formation.

Thermal grooving is particularly valuable, however, in situations where chemical etchants are ineffective, where quantitative boundary-energy data are desired, or where in-situ observation of grain growth at elevated temperatures is the goal.

## 4. EBSD/Kikuchi Pattern Quality from As-Annealed (Unprepared) Surfaces

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) provides powerful capabilities for quantitative grain and grain-boundary characterization, with spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 μm using a field-emission gun SEM (FEGSEM) and automated angular resolution between 0.5° and 1.5° for relative misorientations (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). EBSD enables measurements of grain orientations, boundary misorientations, and coincident site lattice (CSL) boundary fractions that are not obtainable from conventional optical or electron microscopy imaging (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

However, the quality of EBSD Kikuchi patterns is critically dependent on surface condition. The literature strongly indicates that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched, flat, damage-free surfaces (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000012). Surface roughness from etching or thermal grooving degrades diffraction patterns; surface relief that causes one phase to recess below another prevents pattern development from the recessed features (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000013). Scratches and subsurface preparation damage must be completely removed, as the diffraction signal originates from the near-surface layer (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

The importance of final polishing steps has been quantitatively demonstrated: vibratory polishing with colloidal silica improves EBSD band contrast by an average of 11.1% across diverse metals, and for some materials (e.g., pure lead) it is the difference between obtaining no pattern at all versus obtaining indexable patterns (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000032). High-purity metals are generally more difficult to prepare to a damage-free state than commercial alloys (pqac-00000031). Electropolishing is often required for softer metals, though good mechanical polish is sufficient for harder materials (pqac-00000033).

These findings imply that as-annealed surfaces bearing thermal grooves present a challenging scenario for EBSD. The topographic relief introduced by grooving, combined with potential oxide layers formed during high-temperature annealing, would be expected to degrade Kikuchi pattern quality and reduce indexing rates. While the flat grain interiors of well-annealed metals (particularly those with large grains and low dislocation density) might yield analyzable EBSD patterns away from groove features, the groove topography itself would create shadowing artifacts at the steep specimen tilt angles (70–74°) required for EBSD (pqac-00000029). Consequently, if EBSD characterization is the goal, post-annealing metallographic preparation—at minimum a light re-polishing step—is generally advisable to remove groove topography and any surface oxide before EBSD data collection.

At the groove root, a force balance between the grain boundary and the two free surfaces establishes the dihedral angle φ. In the isotropic case, the equilibrium condition yields the classical relation:

sin(φ) = γ_gb / (2γ_s)

This relationship allows the grain-boundary to surface energy ratio to be extracted from measurements of the groove-root dihedral angle (pqac-00000008). The groove depth δ can then be related to the grain radius R and dihedral angle through geometric relationships (pqac-00000023).

When surface energy anisotropy is significant, as in strongly textured nickel films, the equilibrium condition at the groove root must be generalized to account for the orientation-dependence of surface energy. The anisotropic form is:

0.5γ_GB = γ sin(θ_0) + (dγ/dθ) cos(θ_0)

where θ_0 is the maximum surface slope at the groove root, γ is the orientation-dependent surface energy, and the derivative term captures the torque contribution from surface energy anisotropy (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). From this equilibrium expression, the maximum surface slope can be derived as sin(θ_0) = (0.5γ_GB − Δγ)/γ_0, where γ_0 is the surface energy at the singular surface orientation and Δγ represents the anisotropy (pqac-00000007).

For nickel specifically, Amram et al. (2014) fitted experimental groove profiles measured by atomic force microscopy (AFM) to their theoretical model, finding excellent agreement when using representative energy values of γ_0 ≈ 1.8 J m⁻², Δγ ≈ 0.1 J m⁻², and γ_GB ≈ 0.7 J m⁻², with observed groove slopes of approximately 0.14 (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000042). The method has been widely applied to measure relative grain-boundary energies in various polycrystalline materials.

Thermal grooving (also termed thermal etching) provides a route to reveal grain boundaries without recourse to chemical etchants. In polycrystalline thin films more generally, grain-boundary grooves form preferentially at high-energy boundaries and triple junctions, with groove depth varying with local grain-boundary energy (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028). The process is also observed in silver thin films, where thermal grooves at grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for dewetting (pqac-00000020).

Despite these advantages, thermal etching has notable practical drawbacks. Bachmann et al. (2022) noted that in steels, thermal etching requires expensive high-temperature equipment and produces traces of old grooves from grain growth during the heating process, complicating interpretation (pqac-00000011). Chemical etching is generally preferred for routine metallography because it is simpler, less costly, and does not require controlled high-temperature environments (pqac-00000011). Additionally, in thin-film systems, thermal grooving can be complicated by concurrent dewetting, interface diffusion effects, and oxide formation.

Thermal grooving is particularly valuable, however, in situations where chemical etchants are ineffective, where quantitative boundary-energy data are desired, or where in-situ observation of grain growth at elevated temperatures is the goal.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) provides powerful capabilities for quantitative grain and grain-boundary characterization, with spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 μm using a field-emission gun SEM (FEGSEM) and automated angular resolution between 0.5° and 1.5° for relative misorientations (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). The literature strongly indicates that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched, flat, damage-free surfaces (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000012). Scratches and subsurface preparation damage must be completely removed, as the diffraction signal originates from the near-surface layer (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

High-purity metals are generally more difficult to prepare to a damage-free state than commercial alloys (pqac-00000031). Electropolishing is often required for softer metals, though good mechanical polish is sufficient for harder materials (pqac-00000033).

These findings imply that as-annealed surfaces bearing thermal grooves present a challenging scenario for EBSD. The topographic relief introduced by grooving, combined with potential oxide layers formed during high-temperature annealing, would be expected to degrade Kikuchi pattern quality and reduce indexing rates. Consequently, if EBSD characterization is the goal, post-annealing metallographic preparation—at minimum a light re-polishing step—is generally advisable to remove groove topography and any surface oxide before EBSD data collection.

# Grain-Boundary Thermal Grooving in Annealed Metals: Theory, Energy Measurements, Microstructure Revelation, and EBSD Characterization

## 1. Mullins Grooving Theory and Groove Growth Kinetics

The classical theory of grain-boundary thermal grooving was developed by Mullins in 1957, providing the foundational framework for understanding how grooves form where grain boundaries intersect free surfaces during annealing. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism governing groove development, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2). The governing equation for the surface profile evolution is a fourth-order partial differential equation of the form ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient that incorporates surface diffusivity, surface energy, atomic volume, and temperature (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8).

A central prediction of the Mullins theory is that the groove profile exhibits a self-similar shape: all linear dimensions of the groove (depth, width) grow according to the same power law, scaling as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width increase proportional to t^{1/4} (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8, thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 11-13). In the classical model, material is extracted from the groove root and deposited in two characteristic ridges flanking the groove, conserving mass within the groove region; for elemental metals such as nickel, the classical groove width-to-depth ratio is approximately 30 (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 6-7). The time for hole formation through grooving in thin films scales with the fourth power of film thickness: τ_n ∝ h⁴/D_s, where h is the film thickness and D_s is the surface self-diffusivity (thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 11-13).

While surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, Mullins also considered evaporation-condensation as an alternative transport mechanism (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 2-4). However, for most metallic systems, surface diffusion dominates. Mullins introduced a dimensionless parameter r to characterize the ratio of material removed by surface diffusion versus evaporation; when r > 10², surface diffusion is the controlling mechanism (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 2-4).

Important extensions to the classical theory have been developed. Amram et al. (2014) demonstrated that in thin nickel films on sapphire substrates annealed at 700°C, grain-boundary and metal-ceramic interface diffusion contribute significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat, ridge-less grooves that deviate from classical Mullins predictions (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2). Their modified model replaces the classical zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant grain-boundary flux condition and zero curvature at the root, reflecting the fact that grain-boundary and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8). The hierarchy of diffusion paths in crystalline solids, from slowest to fastest, is: bulk diffusion, dislocation core diffusion, grain-boundary diffusion, and surface diffusion (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11).

where θ_0 is the maximum surface slope at the groove root, γ is the orientation-dependent surface energy, and the derivative term captures the torque contribution from surface energy anisotropy (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 8-9, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11). ## 1. Mullins Grooving Theory and Groove Growth Kinetics

The classical theory of grain-boundary thermal grooving was developed by Mullins in 1957, providing the foundational framework for understanding how grooves form where grain boundaries intersect free surfaces during annealing. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism governing groove development, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions (pqac-00000001). The governing equation for the surface profile evolution is a fourth-order partial differential equation of the form ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient that incorporates surface diffusivity, surface energy, atomic volume, and temperature (pqac-00000002).

A central prediction of the Mullins theory is that the groove profile exhibits a self-similar shape: all linear dimensions of the groove (depth, width) grow according to the same power law, scaling as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width increase proportional to t^{1/4} (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000000). In the classical model, material is extracted from the groove root and deposited in two characteristic ridges flanking the groove, conserving mass within the groove region; for elemental metals such as nickel, the classical groove width-to-depth ratio is approximately 30 (pqac-00000004). The time for hole formation through grooving in thin films scales with the fourth power of film thickness: τ_n ∝ h⁴/D_s, where h is the film thickness and D_s is the surface self-diffusivity (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025).

While surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, Mullins also considered evaporation-condensation as an alternative transport mechanism (pqac-00000006). However, for most metallic systems, surface diffusion dominates. Mullins introduced a dimensionless parameter r to characterize the ratio of material removed by surface diffusion versus evaporation; when r > 10², surface diffusion is the controlling mechanism (pqac-00000006).

Important extensions to the classical theory have been developed. Amram et al. (2014) demonstrated that in thin nickel films on sapphire substrates annealed at 700°C, grain-boundary and metal-ceramic interface diffusion contribute significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat, ridge-less grooves that deviate from classical Mullins predictions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000027). Their modified model replaces the classical zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant grain-boundary flux condition and zero curvature at the root, reflecting the fact that grain-boundary and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000021). The hierarchy of diffusion paths in crystalline solids, from slowest to fastest, is: bulk diffusion, dislocation core diffusion, grain-boundary diffusion, and surface diffusion (pqac-00000005).

## 2. Groove Dihedral-Angle Measurement and Grain-Boundary to Surface Energy Ratios

The equilibrium geometry at the groove root provides a direct means of measuring the ratio of grain-boundary energy (γ_gb) to surface energy (γ_s). At the groove root, a force balance between the grain boundary and the two free surfaces establishes the dihedral angle φ. In the isotropic case, the equilibrium condition yields the classical relation:

sin(φ) = γ_gb / (2γ_s)

This relationship allows the grain-boundary to surface energy ratio to be extracted from measurements of the groove-root dihedral angle (pqac-00000008). The groove depth δ can then be related to the grain radius R and dihedral angle through geometric relationships (pqac-00000023).

When surface energy anisotropy is significant, as in strongly textured nickel films, the equilibrium condition at the groove root must be generalized to account for the orientation-dependence of surface energy. The anisotropic form is:

0.5γ_GB = γ sin(θ_0) + (dγ/dθ) cos(θ_0)

where θ_0 is the maximum surface slope at the groove root, γ is the orientation-dependent surface energy, and the derivative term captures the torque contribution from surface energy anisotropy (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). From this equilibrium expression, the maximum surface slope can be derived as sin(θ_0) = (0.5γ_GB − Δγ)/γ_0, where γ_0 is the surface energy at the singular surface orientation and Δγ represents the anisotropy (pqac-00000007).

For nickel specifically, Amram et al. (2014) fitted experimental groove profiles measured by atomic force microscopy (AFM) to their theoretical model, finding excellent agreement when using representative energy values of γ_0 ≈ 1.8 J m⁻², Δγ ≈ 0.1 J m⁻², and γ_GB ≈ 0.7 J m⁻², with observed groove slopes of approximately 0.14 (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000042). The method has been widely applied to measure relative grain-boundary energies in various polycrystalline materials.

## 3. Thermal Grooving as a Means to Reveal Grain Boundaries Without Metallographic Preparation

Thermal grooving (also termed thermal etching) provides a route to reveal grain boundaries without recourse to chemical etchants. During annealing, surface diffusion drives groove formation at grain-boundary/surface junctions, creating topographic features that delineate the grain-boundary network and are readily observable by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), optical microscopy, or AFM (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018).

In nickel thin films, annealing at approximately 700°C produces well-defined grooves that clearly reveal the grain structure, including the mazed bicrystal microstructure characteristic of strongly textured films (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000017). The technique simultaneously provides quantitative information about boundary energetics and diffusion kinetics that chemical etching cannot deliver. In polycrystalline thin films more generally, grain-boundary grooves form preferentially at high-energy boundaries and triple junctions, with groove depth varying with local grain-boundary energy (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028). The process is also observed in silver thin films, where thermal grooves at grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for dewetting (pqac-00000020).

Despite these advantages, thermal etching has notable practical drawbacks. Bachmann et al. (2022) noted that in steels, thermal etching requires expensive high-temperature equipment and produces traces of old grooves from grain growth during the heating process, complicating interpretation (pqac-00000011). Chemical etching is generally preferred for routine metallography because it is simpler, less costly, and does not require controlled high-temperature environments (pqac-00000011). Additionally, in thin-film systems, thermal grooving can be complicated by concurrent dewetting, interface diffusion effects, and oxide formation.

Thermal grooving is particularly valuable, however, in situations where chemical etchants are ineffective, where quantitative boundary-energy data are desired, or where in-situ observation of grain growth at elevated temperatures is the goal.

## 4. EBSD/Kikuchi Pattern Quality from As-Annealed (Unprepared) Surfaces

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) provides powerful capabilities for quantitative grain and grain-boundary characterization, with spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 μm using a field-emission gun SEM (FEGSEM) and automated angular resolution between 0.5° and 1.5° for relative misorientations (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). EBSD enables measurements of grain orientations, boundary misorientations, and coincident site lattice (CSL) boundary fractions that are not obtainable from conventional optical or electron microscopy imaging (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

However, the quality of EBSD Kikuchi patterns is critically dependent on surface condition. The literature strongly indicates that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched, flat, damage-free surfaces (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000012). Surface roughness from etching or thermal grooving degrades diffraction patterns; surface relief that causes one phase to recess below another prevents pattern development from the recessed features (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000013). Scratches and subsurface preparation damage must be completely removed, as the diffraction signal originates from the near-surface layer (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

The importance of final polishing steps has been quantitatively demonstrated: vibratory polishing with colloidal silica improves EBSD band contrast by an average of 11.1% across diverse metals, and for some materials (e.g., pure lead) it is the difference between obtaining no pattern at all versus obtaining indexable patterns (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000032). High-purity metals are generally more difficult to prepare to a damage-free state than commercial alloys (pqac-00000031). Electropolishing is often required for softer metals, though good mechanical polish is sufficient for harder materials (pqac-00000033).

These findings imply that as-annealed surfaces bearing thermal grooves present a challenging scenario for EBSD. The topographic relief introduced by grooving, combined with potential oxide layers formed during high-temperature annealing, would be expected to degrade Kikuchi pattern quality and reduce indexing rates. While the flat grain interiors of well-annealed metals (particularly those with large grains and low dislocation density) might yield analyzable EBSD patterns away from groove features, the groove topography itself would create shadowing artifacts at the steep specimen tilt angles (70–74°) required for EBSD (pqac-00000029). Consequently, if EBSD characterization is the goal, post-annealing metallographic preparation—at minimum a light re-polishing step—is generally advisable to remove groove topography and any surface oxide before EBSD data collection.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a revised Mullins model for grain boundary grooving that incorporates both grain boundary (GB) and interface diffusion, departing from the original Mullins theory which assumed no diffusion flux at the GB root. The model governs the grooving process through a fourth-order partial differential equation: ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient, z is the surface profile, x is the spatial coordinate at the GB location, and t is annealing time. The solution exhibits self-similar kinetics with groove growth following z = m(Bt)^{1/4}F(u), indicating that groove dimensions scale as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width grow as t^{1/4}. The mechanism is surface diffusion, governed by the chemical potential gradient along the surface. The key modification from classical Mullins theory is replacing the zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant GB flux condition and zero curvature at the root, which ensures continuity of diffusion flux when GB and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion.

Exceptional surface flatness is necessary due to the acute angle (70-74°) between specimen and electron beam. The article stresses that surface preparation damage directly influences indexing confidence.

contexts.context: This study examines grain boundary (GB) grooving in annealed nickel thin films, revealing that surface diffusion is the dominant mass-transport mechanism for GB grooving. However, in strongly textured films with low surface defect concentrations, topography-changing surface diffusion is inhibited, increasing the importance of alternative fast diffusion paths like grain boundaries and interfaces. The research demonstrates that both coupled surface and GB diffusion contribute to groove formation, with the observed groove morphology resembling profiles obtained theoretically under in-plane tensile stress. Accumulation of atoms within grain boundaries leads to stress relaxation in the film. The study documents GB groove morphology through AFM topography and STEM microscopy, showing characteristic features like flat-rimmed holes. However, the excerpt does not directly address comparisons with chemical etching methods for revealing grain boundaries.

contexts.context: Thermal grooving in annealed thin nickel films works through grain boundary (GB) grooving, where the local film thickness decreases near grain boundaries due to energy minimization. During annealing at 700°C, grooves form as the system reduces total surface and interface energy. The paper demonstrates that grain boundary self-diffusion plays a crucial role, but significantly, metal-ceramic interface diffusion along the film-substrate boundary is also a critical mass transport mechanism. This interphase boundary diffusion can be as fast as or faster than GB diffusion itself. The authors developed a model incorporating both surface diffusion and metal atom diffusion along the Ni-sapphire interface to explain observed groove shapes that deviated from classical predictions. The simultaneous film thickening observed indicates that atoms diffuse along the interface, creating the characteristic groove topology that reveals grain boundary locations. However, the excerpt does not address comparisons with chemical etching methods for grain boundary revelation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a theoretical model for grain boundary (GB) grooving in thin nickel films during annealing. The study revises the classical Mullins model by incorporating grain boundary and interface diffusion alongside surface diffusion. The key finding is that grain boundary self-diffusion plays a crucial role in groove formation. Unlike the original Mullins model which assumes zero diffusion flux at the GB root, this revised model shows that a constant flux exists at the GB with zero curvature at the root. This occurs because GB and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion. The grooves themselves are identified as the main contributors to film thickening during annealing. The model provides analytical solutions for groove profile evolution over time. contexts.context: The groove depth (δ) formed at grain boundaries depends on the grain radius (R) and the root angle (ϕ), which is determined by a force balance between the grain boundary energy (γgb) and film surface energy (γf). The relationship is expressed as ϕ = sin⁻¹(γgb/2γf) and δ = R(2−3cos ϕ + cos³ϕ)/(3sin³ϕ). The groove profile shape is directly determined by the energies of surfaces meeting at the grain boundary and the grain boundary energy itself. Critically, hole formation and dewetting initiation occurs only when groove depth exceeds film thickness (δ > h). When δ is less than film thickness, grooves remain stable without initiating rupture. The critical grain radius for hole formation is given by a function of these geometric and energetic parameters.

The researchers observed unusually flat, ridge-less grooves in nickel thin films on sapphire that deviated significantly from predictions of the classical Mullins model. The study indicates that for thin polycrystalline metal films on ceramic substrates, the film-substrate interface acts as a fast self-diffusion path that plays an important role in mass transport, fundamentally affecting how grain boundary grooves develop and their resulting topography.

contexts.context: In solid-state dewetting of thin films, grain boundary grooves exhibit inverse scaling with film thickness—the number of holes forming during dewetting scales inversely with film thickness. The groove depth varies with location: grooves at grain boundary triple junctions (where three grain boundaries meet the film surface) are generally deeper than grooves at boundaries between two grains. The groove profile at triple junctions is roughly conical in shape. The groove geometry is determined by the curvature characteristics of grain boundaries in polycrystalline films, which exhibit both in-plane and out-of-plane curvatures similar to catenoid boundaries. These curvatures play a critical role in driving boundary motion and groove formation, with the out-of-plane curvature becoming increasingly important as grooves deepen. The formation and growth of grooves is also influenced by surface energy (γf), grain boundary energy (γgb), and film thickness (h), with lower energy values and thinner films leading to higher areal densities of holes.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses critical surface preparation requirements for EBSD. Surfaces must be kept flat on the plane-of-polish, as relief causing one phase to recess below the surface prevents EBSD pattern development. Scratches and surface damage significantly affect pattern quality, requiring damage-free surfaces for reliable pattern indexing. Vibratory polishing alone improved band contrast by an average of 11.1% across tested elements. contexts.context: EBSD requires an as-polished, non-etched specimen surface with exceptional flatness due to the steep angle (70-74°) between the specimen and electron beam. Surface roughness from etching degrades the diffraction pattern quality. The quality of EBSD patterns depends critically on removal of lattice damage from specimen preparation. contexts.context: The excerpt describes detailed metallographic preparation methods for EBSD analysis of high-purity metals. Surface preparation involves multi-step grinding and polishing procedures, typically five steps (four for Ti). For certain elements susceptible to SiC embedment (Sb, V, Zr), grinding paper was coated with paraffin wax. Attack polishing with 30% H2O2 was used as a final step for Cr, Nb, Ti, W, and Zr. Final polishing employed MasterMet® colloidal silica for most specimens. The excerpt demonstrates that surface condition significantly affects EBSD pattern quality. Chemical polishing of Zr improved polarized light response but introduced excessive relief/grain faceting, which prevented obtaining EBSD patterns on the chemically polished surface. The preparation method directly impacts band contrast and indexable pixel percentages—the improved method achieved 92.34 average band contrast with ~90% indexable pixels versus 77.3 with only ~20% indexable pixels using less effective methods. Vibratory polishing further improved band contrast across multiple high-purity elements.

contexts.context: EBSD provides significant advantages over conventional imaging methods for grain boundary characterization. It offers more accurate grain size measurements than optical or scanning electron microscopy because it uses quantitative definitions of high-angle grain boundaries rather than technique-dependent criteria. EBSD can distinguish between high-angle grain boundaries (HAGB), low-angle grain boundaries (LAGB), and even specific boundary types like coherent twin boundaries, providing detailed information about grain boundary misorientations unavailable from optical or electron microscopy images. Users can selectively include or exclude particular boundary classes with high accuracy. However, EBSD has angular resolution limitations, with a lower detection limit for misorientations (∠L) that may cause problems when characterizing microstructures with small subgrain misorientations. The excerpt shows that EBSD grain size measurements can differ substantially from conventional methods, particularly for textured materials.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses EBSD measurement precision for grain characterization but does not provide specific numerical values for spatial or angular resolution limits. It notes that accuracy limitations arise when grain sizes approach the spatial resolution limit and when subgrain misorientations approach the angular resolution limit of EBSD. The grain reconstruction method offers advantages over the linear intercept method by providing extensive information about grains including area, ECD (Equivalent Circle Diameter), Feret diameters, and aspect ratios. However, grain reconstruction tends to be slower than necessary because most data acquired during EBSD scanning is redundant. The excerpt mentions developing more efficient methods like Adaptive Orientation Image Microscopy to reduce scan time while maintaining similar detail. The precision of measurements depends on sample characteristics, microscope specifications, and data acquisition/analysis modes. Pixel step size relative to grain size is critical for accurate measurement.
contexts.question: What is the spatial resolution and angular resolution of EBSD for grain boundary characterization? How does EBSD compare with other methods for measuring grain orientations and grain boundary character?

contexts.context: EBSD provides spatial resolutions ranging from 9-180 nm depending on the material and microscope type (field emission gun vs. W-filament SEM), with field emission guns offering superior resolution. Angular precision for absolute crystallite orientation is typically ∼2°, though this varies with sample alignment and operating conditions. The angular resolution is influenced by probe current, accelerating voltage, and pattern quality. For characterizing low-angle grain boundaries, the precision of relative orientation measurements between adjacent data points is critical. EBSD represents an automated alternative to standard metallographic methods (optical and scanning electron microscopy) for obtaining grain sizes and shapes. However, limitations exist including non-indexed data points in deformed regions and difficulties determining small misorientations due to orientation noise, which can be quantified through apparent misorientations between data points within the same grain.
contexts.question: What is the spatial resolution and angular resolution of EBSD for grain boundary characterization? How does EBSD compare with other methods for measuring grain orientations and grain boundary character?

snippets: Mullins's theory was widely employed for determining the surface diffusion coefficients from the topography of GB grooves.
Grain boundaries (GBs) represent a key microstructural element of thin metal polycrystalline films and in many cases determine their physical, mechanical and functional properties.

In the process known as GB grooving, the local thickness of the film decreases in the vicinity of a GB. The driving force for this process is the decrease of GB area and concomitant decrease of the total surface/interface energy of the thin film.

contexts.context: This excerpt demonstrates the relationship between thermal grooving and grain boundary energy measurement in nickel. The article develops a model for grain boundary (GB) grooving in thin nickel films that connects groove morphology to GB energy through equilibrium conditions. At the groove root, the GB energy (cGB) relates to surface energy (c) and surface slopes (h0) via equilibrium equations. The authors experimentally measured groove profiles using AFM and fitted them to theoretical predictions, allowing them to determine GB properties. The observed groove slopes in nickel were approximately 0.14, which matched theoretical predictions when assuming specific surface energy values (c0 = 1.8 J m⁻², Δc = 0.1 J m⁻², cGB = 0.7 J m⁻²). However, the excerpt does not explicitly provide a dihedral angle value but instead focuses on surface slopes and energy relationships used to characterize the GB structure.

Question: Review literature on grain-boundary thermal grooving in annealed metals (especially nickel) and its use for microstructure characterization: Mullins grooving theory and groove growth kinetics, groove dihedral-angle measurement of grain-boundary to surface energy ratios, thermal grooving as a way to reveal grain boundaries without metallographic preparation (etching/polishing), and the quality of EBSD/Kikuchi patterns obtainable from as-annealed (unprepared) surfaces. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.

# Grain-Boundary Thermal Grooving in Annealed Metals: Theory, Energy Measurements, Microstructure Revelation, and EBSD Characterization

## 1. Mullins Grooving Theory and Groove Growth Kinetics

The classical theory of grain-boundary thermal grooving was developed by Mullins in 1957, providing the foundational framework for understanding how grooves form where grain boundaries intersect free surfaces during annealing. According to Mullins's model, capillary-driven surface diffusion is the primary mass-transport mechanism governing groove development, particularly for sub-micrometer groove dimensions (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2). The governing equation for the surface profile evolution is a fourth-order partial differential equation of the form ż = Bz'''', where B is the Mullins coefficient that incorporates surface diffusivity, surface energy, atomic volume, and temperature (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8).

A central prediction of the Mullins theory is that the groove profile exhibits a self-similar shape: all linear dimensions of the groove (depth, width) grow according to the same power law, scaling as (Bt)^{1/4}, meaning both depth and width increase proportional to t^{1/4} (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8, thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 11-13). In the classical model, material is extracted from the groove root and deposited in two characteristic ridges flanking the groove, conserving mass within the groove region; for elemental metals such as nickel, the classical groove width-to-depth ratio is approximately 30 (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 6-7). The time for hole formation through grooving in thin films scales with the fourth power of film thickness: τ_n ∝ h⁴/D_s, where h is the film thickness and D_s is the surface self-diffusivity (thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 11-13).

While surface self-diffusion is the dominant mechanism for solid films, Mullins also considered evaporation-condensation as an alternative transport mechanism (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 2-4). However, for most metallic systems, surface diffusion dominates. Mullins introduced a dimensionless parameter r to characterize the ratio of material removed by surface diffusion versus evaporation; when r > 10², surface diffusion is the controlling mechanism (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 2-4).

Important extensions to the classical theory have been developed. Amram et al. (2014) demonstrated that in thin nickel films on sapphire substrates annealed at 700°C, grain-boundary and metal-ceramic interface diffusion contribute significantly to groove formation, producing unusually flat, ridge-less grooves that deviate from classical Mullins predictions (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2). Their modified model replaces the classical zero-flux boundary condition at the groove root with a constant grain-boundary flux condition and zero curvature at the root, reflecting the fact that grain-boundary and interface diffusion are much faster than surface diffusion (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 7-8). The hierarchy of diffusion paths in crystalline solids, from slowest to fastest, is: bulk diffusion, dislocation core diffusion, grain-boundary diffusion, and surface diffusion (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11).

## 2. Groove Dihedral-Angle Measurement and Grain-Boundary to Surface Energy Ratios

The equilibrium geometry at the groove root provides a direct means of measuring the ratio of grain-boundary energy (γ_gb) to surface energy (γ_s). At the groove root, a force balance between the grain boundary and the two free surfaces establishes the dihedral angle φ. In the isotropic case, the equilibrium condition yields the classical relation:

sin(φ) = γ_gb / (2γ_s)

This relationship allows the grain-boundary to surface energy ratio to be extracted from measurements of the groove-root dihedral angle (thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 7-9). The groove depth δ can then be related to the grain radius R and dihedral angle through geometric relationships (thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 7-9).

When surface energy anisotropy is significant, as in strongly textured nickel films, the equilibrium condition at the groove root must be generalized to account for the orientation-dependence of surface energy. The anisotropic form is:

0.5γ_GB = γ sin(θ_0) + (dγ/dθ) cos(θ_0)

where θ_0 is the maximum surface slope at the groove root, γ is the orientation-dependent surface energy, and the derivative term captures the torque contribution from surface energy anisotropy (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 8-9, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11). From this equilibrium expression, the maximum surface slope can be derived as sin(θ_0) = (0.5γ_GB − Δγ)/γ_0, where γ_0 is the surface energy at the singular surface orientation and Δγ represents the anisotropy (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 8-9).

For nickel specifically, Amram et al. (2014) fitted experimental groove profiles measured by atomic force microscopy (AFM) to their theoretical model, finding excellent agreement when using representative energy values of γ_0 ≈ 1.8 J m⁻², Δγ ≈ 0.1 J m⁻², and γ_GB ≈ 0.7 J m⁻², with observed groove slopes of approximately 0.14 (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 8-9, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 9-11). The method has been widely applied to measure relative grain-boundary energies in various polycrystalline materials.

## 3. Thermal Grooving as a Means to Reveal Grain Boundaries Without Metallographic Preparation

Thermal grooving (also termed thermal etching) provides a route to reveal grain boundaries without recourse to chemical etchants. During annealing, surface diffusion drives groove formation at grain-boundary/surface junctions, creating topographic features that delineate the grain-boundary network and are readily observable by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), optical microscopy, or AFM (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 1-2).

In nickel thin films, annealing at approximately 700°C produces well-defined grooves that clearly reveal the grain structure, including the mazed bicrystal microstructure characteristic of strongly textured films (amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 2-4, amram2014grainboundarygrooving pages 4-6). The technique simultaneously provides quantitative information about boundary energetics and diffusion kinetics that chemical etching cannot deliver. In polycrystalline thin films more generally, grain-boundary grooves form preferentially at high-energy boundaries and triple junctions, with groove depth varying with local grain-boundary energy (thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 9-11, thompson2012solidstatedewettingof pages 13-14). The process is also observed in silver thin films, where thermal grooves at grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for dewetting (petersen2008dewettingofni pages 4-5).

Despite these advantages, thermal etching has notable practical drawbacks. Bachmann et al. (2022) noted that in steels, thermal etching requires expensive high-temperature equipment and produces traces of old grooves from grain growth during the heating process, complicating interpretation (bachmann2022efficientreconstructionof pages 2-3). Chemical etching is generally preferred for routine metallography because it is simpler, less costly, and does not require controlled high-temperature environments (bachmann2022efficientreconstructionof pages 2-3). Additionally, in thin-film systems, thermal grooving can be complicated by concurrent dewetting, interface diffusion effects, and oxide formation.

Thermal grooving is particularly valuable, however, in situations where chemical etchants are ineffective, where quantitative boundary-energy data are desired, or where in-situ observation of grain growth at elevated temperatures is the goal.

## 4. EBSD/Kikuchi Pattern Quality from As-Annealed (Unprepared) Surfaces

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) provides powerful capabilities for quantitative grain and grain-boundary characterization, with spatial resolution of approximately 0.1–0.2 μm using a field-emission gun SEM (FEGSEM) and automated angular resolution between 0.5° and 1.5° for relative misorientations (humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 12-13, humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 5-7). EBSD enables measurements of grain orientations, boundary misorientations, and coincident site lattice (CSL) boundary fractions that are not obtainable from conventional optical or electron microscopy imaging (humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 1-2, humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 9-10).

However, the quality of EBSD Kikuchi patterns is critically dependent on surface condition. The literature strongly indicates that EBSD should be performed on as-polished, non-etched, flat, damage-free surfaces (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2). Surface roughness from etching or thermal grooving degrades diffraction patterns; surface relief that causes one phase to recess below another prevents pattern development from the recessed features (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 3-5). Scratches and subsurface preparation damage must be completely removed, as the diffraction signal originates from the near-surface layer (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2, humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 2-3).

The importance of final polishing steps has been quantitatively demonstrated: vibratory polishing with colloidal silica improves EBSD band contrast by an average of 11.1% across diverse metals, and for some materials (e.g., pure lead) it is the difference between obtaining no pattern at all versus obtaining indexable patterns (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 2-3, voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 5-7). High-purity metals are generally more difficult to prepare to a damage-free state than commercial alloys (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 2-3). Electropolishing is often required for softer metals, though good mechanical polish is sufficient for harder materials (humphreys2001reviewgrainand pages 2-3).

These findings imply that as-annealed surfaces bearing thermal grooves present a challenging scenario for EBSD. The topographic relief introduced by grooving, combined with potential oxide layers formed during high-temperature annealing, would be expected to degrade Kikuchi pattern quality and reduce indexing rates. While the flat grain interiors of well-annealed metals (particularly those with large grains and low dislocation density) might yield analyzable EBSD patterns away from groove features, the groove topography itself would create shadowing artifacts at the steep specimen tilt angles (70–74°) required for EBSD (voort2006metallographicpreparationfor pages 1-2). Consequently, if EBSD characterization is the goal, post-annealing metallographic preparation—at minimum a light re-polishing step—is generally advisable to remove groove topography and any surface oxide before EBSD data collection.

artifacts.artifact-01:
| Topic | Key Findings | Key Parameters/Values | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mullins grooving theory fundamentals | Thermal grooves form where a grain boundary meets a free surface because capillarity drives material away from the groove root to reduce total interfacial energy. In the classical Mullins treatment, surface diffusion is the dominant transport path for small grooves, groove shape is self-similar, and mass removed from the root builds adjacent ridges. For elemental metals such as Ni, the classical groove has a large width-to-depth ratio. | Governing evolution is fourth-order diffusion-controlled surface smoothing/grooving; classical self-similar groove dimensions scale together; width-to-depth ratio for classical Mullins grooves is reported as about 30 for elemental metals such as Ni. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000025) |
| Groove growth kinetics | Mullins-type groove growth is diffusion controlled, with all linear dimensions increasing with the same power law. For surface-diffusion-controlled grooving, depth and width scale as \((Bt)^{1/4}\), so groove size follows a \(t^{1/4}\) law. This scaling underlies extraction of surface diffusion information from groove topography; in thin films, added grain-boundary or interface diffusion can accelerate or distort classical kinetics. | Groove depth and width \(\propto (Bt)^{1/4}\); incubation time for hole formation in films \(\tau \propto h^4/D_s\); dominant mechanism in solid films is usually surface self-diffusion rather than evaporation-condensation; modified Ni thin-film models include fast GB/interface diffusion. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000025) |
| Dihedral angle and energy ratio measurement | The equilibrium groove-root angle provides a direct route to the grain-boundary/surface-energy ratio through force balance. In isotropic form, the standard relation is \(\sin(\phi)=\gamma_{gb}/(2\gamma_s)\). In anisotropic form, the equilibrium condition includes the surface-energy derivative with orientation. In annealed Ni thin films, groove-profile fitting gave reasonable energetic values consistent with measured slopes. | Isotropic relation: \(\sin(\phi)=\gamma_{gb}/(2\gamma_s)\); anisotropic relation: \(0.5\gamma_{GB}=\gamma\sin\theta_0+(d\gamma/d\theta)\cos\theta_0\); representative Ni values used in fitting: surface energy \(\gamma_s \approx 1.8\ \text{J m}^{-2}\), grain-boundary energy \(\gamma_{gb} \approx 0.7\ \text{J m}^{-2}\), measured groove slope \(\sim 0.14\). | (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| Thermal grooving for grain boundary revelation | Thermal grooving/thermal etching can reveal grain boundaries without chemical etchants by generating topographic grooves during annealing. In Ni films, grooves directly delineate the grain-boundary network and can be measured by AFM/SEM. Advantages include chemically clean boundary revelation and simultaneous access to boundary energetics/kinetics; disadvantages include need for controlled high-temperature equipment, possible old-groove traces or evolving topography, and in thin films the complication of dewetting or interface-diffusion effects. Chemical etching is often simpler and cheaper for routine metallography. | Ni thin-film example: annealing at about 700 °C revealed GB grooves; groove morphology in Ni/sapphire deviated from classical Mullins behavior because interface diffusion contributed strongly; thermal etching in steels is useful but can leave traces of older grooves and needs specialized equipment. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027) |
| EBSD pattern quality and surface preparation requirements | The literature strongly indicates that EBSD is best performed on flat, damage-free, as-polished, non-etched surfaces. Surface relief, roughness, preferential attack, and preparation damage degrade Kikuchi patterns and indexing, so thermally grooved or otherwise topographic surfaces are generally unfavorable for high-quality EBSD unless subsequently repolished. Vibratory polishing materially improves pattern quality. EBSD remains powerful for grain-boundary characterization when preparation is adequate. | Vibratory polishing improved band contrast by about 11.1% on average; FEGSEM EBSD spatial resolution is about 0.1–0.2 µm; automated EBSD angular resolution is about 0.5–1.5° for relative misorientation; flat specimens tilted about 70–74° are required; etched/recessed phases may fail to yield patterns. | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038) |

info.query: Review literature on grain-boundary thermal grooving in annealed metals (especially nickel) and its use for microstructure characterization: Mullins grooving theory and groove growth kinetics, groove dihedral-angle measurement of grain-boundary to surface energy ratios, thermal grooving as a way to reveal grain boundaries without metallographic preparation (etching/polishing), and the quality of EBSD/Kikuchi patterns obtainable from as-annealed (unprepared) surfaces. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.
